To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
most of the N applied in a fertigated banana plantation is lost by leaching, and this loss occurs mainly in the summer when irrigation is applied.

the hydrological and chemical processes occurring in the system, together with the irrigation and fertigation management, produce an annual N loss of 202–218 g/ha, which is diluted around 60–70% before reaching the coastal aquifer.

(1) the high water fluxes in the soil profile and the high N application rates produce a high N loss (50–60%) in the drainage water and (2) a large part of the N lixiviates is diluted by the lateral flow before it reaches the polluted aquifer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fate and transport of N in a fertigated banana plantation in the Canary Islands (Spain), and the hydrogeological and hydrological behavior of a thin soil profile on top of fractured basalt.
the hydrological behavior, and the fate of nitrate in a sprinkler fertigated agricultural area in the Canary Islands, where the aquifer is already polluted.
the quantification of N losses from a sprinkler fertigated crop, the fate of the N in the soil profile and the aquifer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the system is very efficient in terms of N uptake, but it is very inefficient in terms of water and N use efficiency, and the system is very sensitive to the N application rate and timing.

the system is highly vulnerable to nitrate pollution, and that the main cause of the problem is not the irrigation system itself, but the high N application rates and the low soil infiltration capacity.
, although the system is highly vulnerable to pollution, the actual nitrate leaching is not very high (around 50%) due to the dilution of the lixiviates with lateral flow.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hydrogeological conditions in the area favor the rapid movement of water and nitrate from the soil to the aquifer and, consequently, to the sea.
the high N losses are produced by high N applications, high irrigation rates, and high water fluxes through preferential pathways.
the soil is a very efficient filter for the nitrate removal, and the aquifer is not being polluted by the banana crop.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the soil profile and the fractured aquifer are very efficient filters of nitrate lixiviation, and therefore, the aquifer is not at risk.

a detailed hydrogeological study is required before any attempt to understand and quantify N degradation and transport in the soil profile, and that it is necessary to consider the mixing of irrigation drainage and lateral flow when estimating the N fluxes to the aquifer.

the hydrogeological setting of this area, together with the high N input and the high irrigation rates, produce a fast and high nitrate lixiviation to the aquifer, which is diluted by the lateral flow.
